items.title: AI is automating most SRE incident responses but may reduce human expertise for handling complex failures, raising concerns about deskilling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A recent analysis highlights that while AI currently automates about 95% of routine incident responses in site reliability engineering (SRE), this shift may be deskilling human engineers by limiting their exposure to complex, novel failures. The article draws parallels to industrial automation's impact on blue-collar workers, where automation reduced hands-on practice and degraded critical intervention skills during rare crises. Current AI applications in SRE include alert noise reduction, runbook execution for known issues, anomaly detection, and auto-remediation for common failures. Future developments aim to enhance multi-signal correlation, autonomous root-cause analysis, predictive incident detection, and AI-driven change risk assessments. However, as AI handles more routine tasks, human SREs may only engage with the most complex incidents, potentially eroding their intuition and expertise needed for effective response. This trend raises questions about the long-term implications for SRE capabilities and system reliability, emphasizing the need to balance automation benefits with maintaining human skills essential for managing unprecedented outages.

items.title: OpenAI raises less than half of $30 billion funding target in latest round
items.content_text: OpenAI has secured less than half of its $30 billion fundraising goal in its most recent funding round. The shortfall highlights challenges the company faces in meeting its ambitious capital targets amid evolving market conditions.

items.title: Cisco president Jeetu Patel gives 27-year-old engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite legacy code, aiming to refactor 98% within 24 months [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Cisco president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel has empowered a 27-year-old engineer, Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, with unlimited AI tokens to overhaul the company's legacy code. Krishnamurthy, a former startup founder acquired by Cisco, was previously underutilized but is now leading a project to refactor nearly all legacy code within two years. Patel emphasizes the value of fresh perspectives from younger employees and seeks to recruit more young talent to challenge established practices. He encourages tension and collaboration between newer and veteran staff to foster innovation, viewing early-career workers as essential for injecting new ideas and driving transformation within the company.

items.title: Phorion detects persistent SSH backdoor in official Claude Code VS Code extension on Cursor Marketplace, prompting removal and incident response advisories
items.content_text: Phorion discovered a backdoor in the official Claude Code extension for Visual Studio Code distributed via the Cursor Marketplace, which installs a persistent SSH backdoor on macOS, Linux, and Windows systems. The compromised extension was removed from the marketplace and related registries after the discovery, and organizations using version 2.1.313 are urged to review their environments and engage incident response. The backdoor operates by appending an attacker-controlled SSH public key to the authorized_keys file and attempts to enable SSH services on affected systems, though some platform-specific bugs limit its effectiveness, such as a macOS check that fails to enable Remote Login without root privileges. The extension runs malicious code immediately upon loading, granting attackers potential long-term interactive access to local files and developer tools without user interaction. Despite some implementation errors that reduce impact on macOS and Windows, the malware remains a significant threat due to its persistence mechanisms and host reconnaissance capabilities. Users and administrators should monitor for signs of compromise and take appropriate remediation steps.

items.title: LRMoE introduces memory-aware load recalibration for efficient Mixture-of-Experts training on GPU nodes with limited memory, reducing training time by up to 44.8% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: LRMoE is a new training system designed to optimize sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models on memory-constrained GPU nodes by recalibrating backward demand and balancing workload retention. It plans retention quotas and expert placement during forward execution and uses a load recalibration metric during backpropagation to select token-expert pairs within resource limits, reducing communication and computation overhead. The system employs a capacity-aware routing algorithm and physical compaction techniques to minimize backward traffic and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on large-scale models Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B demonstrate that LRMoE cuts cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2% to 44.8% compared to existing methods like SYMI.

items.title: Researchers develop amortized localized posterior inference method for model calibration, applying it to ocean turbulence closure to reduce predictive errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a method for model calibration that constructs localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods based on proximity to target contexts, accounting for uncertainties in observations and contexts. They use Gaussian localization weights with covariance inflation and approximate the posteriors via conditional normalizing flows through amortized variational inference. This approach integrates localized posteriors to produce marginalized parameter distributions, aiming to address model discrepancies across context domains. In experiments with the Branin-Hoo model, the localized inference method reduced aggregate predictive errors compared to global posterior inference under both uniform and skewed context distributions. Applying the method to the k-ε turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, showed that localized posterior calibration decreased temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration methods. The experiments were designed to allow local compensation, demonstrating the method's effectiveness in improving model calibration in complex physical systems.

items.title: ThinkJev introduces a hybrid system combining fast and slow reasoning for calibrated typed decisions, optimizing accuracy and computational cost on Qwen3.5 models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: ThinkJev presents a method that uses a single language model to produce typed decisions either directly or after a reasoning step, balancing speed and accuracy. The system employs two modes: System 1 answers quickly using initial probabilities, while System 2 refines answers after additional thought, allowing adaptive computation based on confidence levels without extra training. Evaluations on Qwen3.5 models show that ThinkJev meets target error rates while reducing computation by selectively applying reasoning, achieving accuracy comparable to always thinking but with fewer thought tokens used. The approach was tested on JevBench, an independent typed-decision benchmark, where it performed similarly to existing thinking APIs, and the code and data are publicly available.

items.title: OpenFrontiers releases a cross-disciplinary corpus of 12,151 open research problems and a benchmark of 200 math problems for evaluating scientific rediscovery by large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenFrontiers introduces a structured dataset combining over 12,000 open research problems with a benchmark of 200 recently resolved or still open mathematical problems, each formally verified and reviewed. The resource aims to facilitate evaluation of large language models (LLMs) on research-level problem solving by providing problem statements, context, progress, and formal proof verification under various conditions. The benchmark includes a high-quality subset of 50 problems and uses an evaluation protocol with independent proof checkers in sandboxed environments under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web settings. Testing seven LLM agents showed that closed-book rediscovery of solutions is rare, while live-web success mainly reflects retrieval of existing published solutions. OpenFrontiers offers a foundation for measuring progress in scientific problem solving and is available on Hugging Face.

items.title: WebAnything launches automated framework to reconstruct reusable web environments from real URLs for scalable agent training and evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: WebAnything introduces a fully automated system that creates source-grounded, reusable web environments from real URLs without requiring manual per-site engineering or repairs after initial setup. The framework uses an Explorer-Builder to collect browser-observable data and an independent verifier to ensure fidelity and guide repairs, enabling reproducible training and evaluation of web agents across diverse sites. The team constructed 244 website artifacts spanning 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting nearly 13,000 executed tasks. In a blind audit, WebAnything outperformed the human-assisted WebHarbor on three fidelity metrics. Fine-tuning the Qwen3.5-9B model on interaction trajectories collected by WebAnything improved success rates by up to 13.33 percentage points on standard benchmarks, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness for scalable web agent environments.

items.title: Study compares curated, LLM-generated, and data-derived ontologies as error checkers for LLM agents querying knowledge graphs, analyzing accuracy and false positives across public and private datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers evaluated the effectiveness of different ontology sources-curated, generated by large language models (LLMs), and derived from data-in checking answers produced by LLM agents querying knowledge graphs. They tested these ontologies as prompt context, checkers, or both, across open-weight and proprietary agents on public graphs and a private graph with nearly one billion triples, measuring which errors were caught and which correct answers were wrongly flagged. The study found that curated ontologies, such as the one used for UniProt, flagged more correct answers than LLM-derived or data-derived ontologies, but their precision was only slightly better than random. It also revealed that curated schemas can contradict their own data and that combining ontology sources or providing specific feedback to agents may influence error detection. These findings highlight limitations in relying solely on ontologies as reliable judges of LLM agent outputs over knowledge graphs.

items.title: Researchers measure where AI-written smart contracts lose intended behavior and propose an elicitation-first approach to recover missing requirements [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied the gap between AI-generated smart contract code and the intended behavior described in plain English, focusing on contracts that manage blockchain transactions and cannot be altered once deployed. They developed an evaluation method that compares the execution of AI-written contracts against original contracts by replaying transactions and measuring agreement, revealing that common evaluation tools miss many errors. The team introduced an elicitation-first architecture where AI agents ask clients clarifying questions before coding, check contracts against independently written executable answer keys, and report discrepancies instead of silently fixing code, which proved more effective than post-generation reviews or automated patches across multiple AI models.

items.title: Researchers propose Partner-Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi) to detect covert communication codes between AI agents by comparing behavioral responses to message rewording in simulated markets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Partner-Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi), a behavioral test designed to detect secret communication codes between AI agents that appear as innocent messages. PoPLi measures the difference in how a partner agent using a code and an uninvolved agent respond to reworded messages with the same meaning, computed by replaying logged prompts. In simulated market experiments with various conditions, PoPLi reliably identified the presence of covert first-letter codes, while traditional message-only monitors failed to distinguish collusion scenarios. The study tested five market conditions including no collusion, joint rewards with neutral or openly stated intentions, and covert codes with or without stated intentions. PoPLi values ranged from 0.48 to 0.59 when codes were present and near zero or negative without codes, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting private communication channels. However, PoPLi does not detect collusion based solely on incentives or codes embedded in message meaning, highlighting its specific focus on identifying covert signaling rather than collusion in general.

items.title: Researchers introduce LibStructBench to evaluate AI agents' ability to reconstruct sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows, finding current models struggle with exact molecular-state and workflow accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed LibStructBench, a new benchmark designed to assess AI agents' capability to accurately reconstruct molecular structures and workflows from sequencing protocols, a key task for analyzing customized sequencing assays. Their experiments reveal that while leading AI agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions, they remain unreliable in achieving exact molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. The study found that changing the underlying language model had a greater impact on performance than altering the agent framework, with significant differences observed only in molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved recovery of oligo families in a small pilot but did not enhance overall molecular workflow scores. Attempts to autonomously accumulate procedural rules and cross-protocol examples resulted in inconsistent validation performance and no improvement in held-out molecular workflows, underscoring the need for more controlled and verifiable scientific reasoning methods in complex molecular protocol analysis.

items.title: Researchers introduce Seq@K, a new evaluation protocol measuring language models' ability to solve problems through sequential feedback and iterative refinement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose Seq@K, an evaluation method that tests whether language models can solve problems within K sequential attempts using feedback after each failure, addressing limitations of existing metrics like Pass@K. They evaluated Seq@K across seven benchmarks and sixteen models, finding it reveals different model rankings and more efficient configurations compared to traditional metrics. The study also analyzes how models refine answers based on feedback and emphasizes the importance of designing effective feedback loops for iterative agentic systems.

items.title: Researchers analyze visual representations of Indian cuisine to assess food similarity beyond identity using multiple pretrained models and an expanded Khana dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied how different visual representations organize Indian foods into relational neighborhoods, revealing or obscuring culinary relationships beyond simple identity preservation. They used seven pretrained models, including convolutional, transformer-based, self-supervised, and image-text aligned models, to evaluate image-to-image retrieval and image-to-dish neighborhoods, focusing on culinary-family structure and cross-representation agreement. The study found substantial variation in image-level neighborhoods across representations, including similarities crossing culinary-family boundaries. Aggregated dish-level visual similarity showed common structure despite local variation but correlated less strongly with recipe-derived similarity. These results indicate that food similarity depends on representation, modality, and abstraction level, suggesting that recognition performance alone cannot capture relational structure and that understanding these factors is essential for integrating multiple food information modalities into a coherent similarity framework.

items.title: Verification Learning Theory models how perceived AI assistant reliability affects evidence checking and rule retention in AI-assisted judgment tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Verification Learning Theory (VLT) proposes a process model linking perceived reliability of AI assistance to the frequency of evidence checking and subsequent retention of decision rules in independent judgment. The theory predicts that perceiving AI as fallible can improve delayed unaided judgments by encouraging more checking, even without observed errors, but this benefit disappears when checking is already mandatory and performed. The model assumes that learning depends solely on checking behavior and that each genuine check contributes equally to rule retention. Simulations explore the model's implications and parameter sensitivities, while comparisons with other cognitive theories highlight where predictions differ or align. The framework also outlines experiments to test the mechanism and distinguishes between retaining practiced rules and recognizing which rule applies to new claims.

items.title: Researchers analyze when and how socio-demographic information improves pluralistic offensiveness modeling, highlighting the role of explicit reasoning in enhancing prediction accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This study examines the impact of incorporating annotators' socio-demographic data into pluralistic offensiveness models, addressing mixed prior findings by analyzing effectiveness and mechanisms across three multi-annotator datasets using large language models. The researchers find that demographic information yields small, inconsistent gains at the individual level but clearer benefits when aggregated at group and population levels, as aggregation reduces individual variation that obscures demographic signals. They also show that explicit reasoning, which separates baseline judgments from demographic-specific deviations, improves both baseline estimation and demographic shifts, leading to better final predictions compared to direct demographic conditioning. These results suggest that the value of socio-demographic information depends on evaluation methods and model guidance, explaining previous inconsistent evidence.

items.title: Researchers introduce FilingLoop, a self-evolving LLM agent framework and benchmark for reviewing and revising corporate disclosures using SEC correspondence from 96 companies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: FilingLoop is an interactive benchmark and agent framework designed to support language model agents in reviewing and revising corporate disclosures by identifying deficiencies, acquiring missing facts, and verifying revisions against evidence-backed requirements. It reconstructs 380 IPO review tasks from historical SEC correspondence and evaluates filings against over 6,000 requirements, auditing unsupported claims and harmful revisions. The framework enables iterative review and revision within cases and procedural learning across cases without updating model weights, allowing adaptation to be assessed on new tasks. In evaluations, FilingLoop improved requirement fulfillment from 24.28% to 27.96% and full comment resolution from 16.90% to 20.75%, with a modest increase in cost compared to a fixed policy. This approach links discovered concerns, company facts, and committed revisions, providing detailed feedback to improve future review procedures.

items.title: Researchers introduce HRF-Res, a spiking reservoir computing model using frequency-selective Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire neurons to improve classification accuracy and energy efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed HRF-Res, a liquid state machine that replaces traditional Leaky Integrate-and-Fire neurons with Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire neurons exhibiting intrinsic oscillatory dynamics. This design enables the reservoir to selectively respond to input frequencies, capturing frequency-specific temporal patterns and improving classification accuracy without compromising energy efficiency. Evaluated on ten benchmarks including time series, sequential images, audio spike trains, and neuromorphic vision, HRF-Res achieved state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods while consuming up to 19 times less energy than comparable non-spiking oscillatory reservoirs.

items.title: Researchers introduce SciGame benchmark for evaluating scientific discovery agents using real and counterfactual environments with historical and temporal scientific laws [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed SciGame, a controlled benchmark that transforms scientific literature into structured scientific cards, each providing paired original and counterfactual environments for testing AI agents in scientific discovery tasks. SciGame includes a historical collection of canonical laws and a temporal collection from recent papers, evaluating agents under various protocols in identification and discovery settings. Experiments with five advanced models revealed that familiar priors can hinder performance when underlying relations change, adaptive experimentation benefits stronger models but can harm weaker ones under limited resources, and accurate explanations may mask quantitative errors. While current agents can actively investigate systems, accurately inducing exact symbolic laws in new contexts remains a significant challenge.

items.title: VerifiedLab: Harnessing Knowns for Unknowns [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.37923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Across human history, knowledge has undergone several transitions, from orality to writing and then to digital archives. At each transition, humans established new conventions to preserve knowledge for the new era. Nowadays, as research agents are increasingly deployed for laboratory experiments, knowledge is crossing another boundary: from records written for humans to those for machines. In this work, we introduce VerifiedLab, a multi-agent harness framework for this human-to-machine transition of knowledge. VerifiedLab transforms research output from passive artifacts into active systems that accelerate downstream use, adoption and prediction of future trends. In VerifiedLab, a team of AI scientists with distinct roles reasons over records verified field by field: a principal investigator plans, a librarian computes the evidence directly from the records, specialists draft, and a gate and a critic check each claim against the measured reliability of its data before the harness decides whether to release or withhold it. We demonstrate the efficacy of VerifiedLab through extensive experiments on perovskite solar cells: VerifiedLab recovers known physical trends, anticipates devices reported a year later, and lets AI scientists inherit the literature together with a measure of how far it can be trusted. By scaling the inference-time verification compute, VerifiedLab introduces a new pathway for knowledge dissemination and machine harness for AI co-scientists.

items.title: GARDEN: Generalist Autonomous Reward Design Through Evidence Navigation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.37926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.

items.title: Understanding Large Language Models as Numerical Optimizers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.37932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as potential tools for numerical optimization. Despite promising results, their intrinsic optimization capabilities and limitations remain poorly understood, particularly in high dimensions. This paper investigates the ability of LLMs to exploit mathematical problem structures and generate feasible, near-optimal solutions. We develop an evaluation framework that distinguishes solution quality from execution failures, including numerical inaccuracies, constraint violations, and output-format errors. Using representative problems from convex optimization, fractional programming, and constrained projection, we assess LLM performance against deterministic reference solvers across different dimensions. Our results reveal that LLMs can capture useful optimization structures and produce near-optimal solutions, even when their outputs fail to satisfy numerical or formatting requirements. However, reliability deteriorates with increasing problem dimension and depends strongly on the underlying optimization structure. To further investigate the limitations, we deploy an iterative refinement mechanism that provides targeted feedback on feasibility and solution quality. The results demonstrate that iterative refinement substantially improves reliability and extends the range of problem dimensions over which LLMs produce valid solutions. Nevertheless, persistent numerical and structural errors limit their applicability as standalone optimizers. These findings provide insights into the capacity and limits of LLM-based optimization and motivate hybrid approaches that combine LLM reasoning with deterministic numerical verification.

items.title: SkillMem: Compact External Skill Memory for Latent Multi-Agent Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.37935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.

items.title: GAUSS: A Workload-Aware Analytical and Monte-Carlo Simulator for LLM Inference Serving [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.37989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has become an operational workload that fleets must provision, monitor, and bill against latency service-level objectives (SLOs). A single throughput number cannot answer the questions operators actually face, because generative serving couples two phases with very different service characteristics, continuous batching reshapes the effective service process, and user-visible tail latency can degrade long before aggregate throughput saturates. We present GAUSS, a workload-aware analytical and Monte-Carlo simulator that predicts the full distributions of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT), together with the sustainable request rate, for a given workload, engine, and accelerator. GAUSS pairs calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode with a Lindley-recurrence model of queueing under stochastic arrivals and estimates performance by ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling rather than by replaying a single trace. This lets GAUSS reason about workloads, routing policies, and hardware that have never been deployed, and to capture the latency tails that trace-driven simulators systematically under-sample. We describe the model and show how it supports operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling capacity questions that trace-driven simulators cannot address.

items.title: Algorithmic Bias from the Perspectives of Healthcare Professionals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper focuses on algorithmic bias of machine learning and artificial intelligence applications in healthcare information systems. Based on the quantitative data and qualitative comments from a survey and interviews with healthcare professionals, who have different job roles (e.g., clinical vs. administrative), this study provides findings about the relationships between algorithmic bias, perceived fairness, and the intended acceptance and adoption of ML algorithms and algorithm generated outcomes. The results suggest that the opinions of healthcare professionals toward the causes of algorithmic bias, the criteria of algorithm assessment, the perceived fairness, and bias mitigation approaches may vary depending on their job roles, perspectives, tasks, and the algorithm characteristics. More research is needed to investigate algorithmic bias to ensure fairness and equality in healthcare.

items.title: Assessing Language Models for Scientific Applications: Inertial Confinement Fusion as a Use Case [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advancing language models for specialized scientific applications requires evaluations of scientific fluency, physical reasoning, and quantitative analyses. Using inertial confinement fusion (ICF) as a test case, we have developed an expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions spanning qualitative reasoning, numerical calculation, symbolic derivation, and equation formulation. Responses have been evaluated using deterministic numerical and symbolic checks together with language-model judges. We compared a variety of out-of-the-box closed-source and open-source large language models with Prospero, a model specialized through combined domain-adaptive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning for ICF. We also conducted initial retrieval-assisted evaluations. Prospero improved its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model, with gains across all question types. Frontier models achieved the highest aggregate scores, but critical physics errors persisted, particularly in numerical calculations. We note that domain-specific performance can improve through specialization, but benchmark gains alone do not establish scientific reliability. Retrieval improved performance for a smaller model but yielded no statistically significant improvement for a frontier model. Two scientific stress tests further illustrate useful capabilities and the need for expert assessment of physical assumptions and model validity. Based on these findings, we recommend evaluating existing domain capabilities and retrieval benefits before committing to substantial additional specialization.

items.title: PromptSense: Sentiment-Aware Mental Health Chatbot with Dynamic Prompting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current Large Language Models (LLMs)-based mental health chatbots often lack sufficient empathy, contextual awareness, and safety mechanisms, potentially leading to ineffective or harmful interactions. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates sentiment and depression analysis with a rule-based filtering mechanism prior to model inference. By dynamically constructing prompts based on emotional and risk-related insights, the framework aims to significantly improve the contextual relevance, empathy, and risk-aware of model-generated responses. We evaluated four model strategies and two prompt engineered variants across qualitative metrics such as empathy, helpfulness, clarity, relevance, safety, as well as toxicity assessments using the Perspective API. Experimental results indicate that the prompt engineering approaches outperforms DSFT and RLAIF by 1.8\% and 1.1\% respectively.

items.title: Evaluating Causal Reasoning in LLMs: A Case Study in the Challenges of Procedural Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) appear to represent and reason about a large range of phenomena. In particular, recent studies have examined whether LLMs can accurately reason about causation. One of the most commonly used benchmarks for evaluating formal causal reasoning in LLMs is CLadder, a framework for procedural generation of benchmark data sets that was released in 2023. Experiments with CLadder appear to indicate that LLMs can perform formal causal reasoning in a large percentage of generated examples. In this paper, we examine what can be reliably inferred when LLMs perform well on test sets produced by CLadder. We identify several examples of superficial and highly predictive patterns that the CLadder generator embeds in data sets it generates. We find that even simple models such as random forests perform well on CLadder-generated data sets after training on a sample of generated data. We also find that the performance of many commercial LLMs on CLadder test sets is extremely brittle and that removing large sections of the text that are critical for formal causal reasoning has almost no effect on performance. Given these results, the most likely hypothesis for the strong performance of state-of-the-art LLMs on CLadder is that they are exploiting superficial patterns learned from exposure to training data from the generator. Any inference that LLMs are exhibiting more complex causal reasoning must rule out this hypothesis.

items.title: AI-Driven Digital Twin Framework for Warehouse Logistics Automation Optimization [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, warehouse logistics optimization has increasingly focused on intelligent, data-driven systems to enhance operational efficiency. Conventional static product placement strategies are being progressively replaced by dynamic slotting approaches that can adapt to real-time variations in warehouse conditions. In this work, we present a novel framework that employs a reinforcement learning agent integrated within a FlexSim-based Digital Twin environment for real-time product placement optimization. The proposed agent continuously learns from streaming operational data, enabling it to reduce picking time while improving overall system throughput. The simulation environment models a four-zone warehouse layout with forklift-based material handling and leverages the Asset Administration Shell framework to ensure seamless interaction between the learning agent, physical asset, and the digital twin. Experimental evaluation demonstrates substantial performance gains, with the proposed approach achieving a 29.66\% reduction in average picking time, a 35.42\% increase in throughput, and an 18.54\% decrease in travel distance.

items.title: Too Hard, Too Easy, Just Right: Performance-Driven Challenge Adaptation in Virtual Reality Firefighter Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective firefighter training requires practice under dynamic and stressful emergency conditions, yet real-world live-fire exercises are costly, risky, and difficult to scale. Virtual Reality (VR) offers a safe and controllable alternative, but many existing VR firefighter training systems rely on fixed scenarios or provide limited difficulty adaptation, making it difficult to maintain an appropriate level of challenge for skill development as trainees' performance changes over time. To address this limitation, we present ProACT, a performance-driven adaptive training system that regulates scenario difficulty through closed-loop interactions between trainee performance and simulated fire dynamics. Specifically, ProACT combines a global module that continuously adjusts scene-level fire spread dynamics in real time based on trainee performance with a local module that periodically updates object-level flammability across the environment. Our evaluation shows that ProACT improves both objective training performance and subjective user experience compared with existing adaptive and non-adaptive baselines. We further discuss how adaptive immersive environments can extend beyond firefighting to broader training domains.

items.title: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.

items.title: Decompose, Don't Expand: Capability-Independent AI Systems by Construction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A recurring design choice in building AI systems is whether, when a task is too hard for a model, to expand the model (make it larger, better-prompted, fine-tuned), or to decompose the task (extract the parts that admit a deterministic solution to a host, leaving the model only the irreducibly fuzzy residue). We make three claims. First, that many tasks commonly delegated whole to a model are in fact deterministic tasks with a small generative core. Second, and our central empirical result, that decomposing such a task yields a measurable and desirable property we call parity by construction: on the extracted sub-tasks the model-size performance curve becomes flat, because no model performs them at all. We measure this across nine models spanning a 494M-parameter local checkpoint to a frontier Opus-class model, a thirty-fold parameter range on the local family alone: once the host resolves the context, operation selection scores identically for all nine models and selector resolution for eight of nine, while the one task that does not decompose, labelling, remains sloped across the same range. Because the task leaves the model, a stock checkpoint suffices: no task-specific training and no fine-tuning. Third, that this is a general design discipline, not a domain trick: we show the same move recurring across physics setup, motion retargeting, and object-model editing, and in a Web-CLI tool family (same author, so not an independent replication). We give a method for locating the cut, the construction that makes a cut exist (a deterministic surface and a closed grammar over it), and a way to make the residue safe (resolve the deterministic context; verify the generative output), position the work against neuro-symbolic AI, tool-augmented language models, and generate-and-verify approaches, and are explicit about what is measured (one domain) versus illustrative (the rest).

items.title: SkillCT: A Multidimensional Benchmark and Execution-Free Baseline for Agent Skill Assessment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills package instructions, scripts, and resources for specialized tasks and are increasingly distributed through public Web repositories. However, existing skill benchmarks primarily focus on downstream task execution, insufficiently assessing specification quality, behavioral robustness, semantic alignment, and responsibility boundaries. Their reliance on task-specific tools, environments, and repeated executions limits scalability and pre-deployment assessment. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillCT, a benchmark that broadens skill assessment from downstream utility to a multidimensional characterization of skill quality. SkillCT evaluates skills across nine complementary dimensions spanning three aspects: Static Assessment, which captures intrinsic properties of the skill specification; Dynamic Assessment, which measures whether the induced behavior remains stable across backbone models and request variations; and Human-Assisted Assessment, which examines behavior-chain consistency and task granularity. These dimensions provide a broader view of skill quality than execution success. Applying SkillCT to a public skill corpus establishes a reference benchmark for analyzing quality weaknesses and relationships across dimensions. Building on this benchmark, we propose an execution-free quality evaluation baseline that predicts the multidimensional quality profiles of unseen skills by retrieving and leveraging similar reference skills, without executing the skills under evaluation. This reduces token consumption and evaluation time, while preserving consistency with the full assessment. Furthermore, SkillCT-guided optimization improves downstream task success and execution efficiency, demonstrating its value for skill refinement. These findings highlight the effectiveness of SkillCT in supporting scalable skill assessment, optimization, and repository maintenance.

items.title: BridgeRouter: Gain-Aware Instance Routing over Cross-Modal Bridge Portfolios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lightweight representation bridges make pretrained, task-adapted EEG foundation models executable on other biosignal modalities without retraining their backbones. However, selecting a single bridge pathway globally assigns every instance to the same transfer route and ignores complementary errors across routes. We therefore formulate multi-bridge transfer as an instance-level algorithm-selection problem and introduce BridgeRouter, a gain-aware router over a portfolio of frozen cross-modal pathways. A validation-selected Single Best Solver (SBS) serves as a protected default route. During training, task labels are used to compute the reduction in negative log-likelihood provided by each alternative route relative to the SBS, and a lightweight MLP predicts these route-specific gains from a target-modality representation extracted by a frozen encoder. At inference, BridgeRouter observes only the target modality, requires neither EEG, task labels, nor predictions from all candidate routes, and executes exactly one bridge pathway: the route with the largest predicted gain when that gain exceeds a validation-calibrated threshold, and the SBS otherwise. We evaluate seven EEG foundation-model bridge pathways for EMG-based freezing-of-gait detection on FOG and ECG-based sleep classification on ISRUC. Across five seeds, BridgeRouter achieves $81.38\pm1.11\%$ balanced accuracy on FOG, improving over the BIOT SBS by $11.49$ percentage points, and $62.92\pm2.17\%$ on ISRUC, improving over the CBraMod SBS by $3.83$ points. Per-instance bridge oracles reach $99.96\%$ and $78.61\%$, respectively, revealing substantial remaining portfolio headroom. These results show that anchor-relative gain prediction can convert complementary cross-modal bridge behavior into deployable instance-level routing improvements while retaining single-route inference.

items.title: DecompGym: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Designing Decomposition Algorithms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Benders decomposition and column generation solve large optimization problems by passing cuts, columns, and dual values between a master problem and subproblems, and are hard to implement correctly. Large language models now automate parts of algorithm design, which points toward agents that build decomposition solvers for new problems. As a first step toward such agents, we study how well current coding agents design and implement these two algorithms, and how they fail. We introduce DecompGym, 81 instances from nine problem families (five Benders, four column generation), in which an agent writes a solver for a prescribed method. Each solver must meet three criteria: execution within a 60-second time limit; numerical feasibility together with a method audit, in which an LLM judge reads the solver's code; and an objective within 1% of the stored optimal objective. We evaluate 12 GPT, Claude, and Gemini models running in coding-agent tools. Over up to ten attempts, we compare independent regeneration with reflection, which first diagnoses the failure. On the first attempt, two models solve every instance and seven solve more than 90%. Most Benders failures (48 of 62) are missing or suboptimal solutions. The most common column-generation failure is a method-audit rejection. Output checks alone would accept 93 of the 108 attempts that fail the method audit. The most common rejection, an optimalif, occurs 96 times, 92 of them in one model.Reflection turns 66% of retries into successes, compared with 39% for regeneration, and it repairs method-audit failures, for which the judge names the defecective gaps. Agents for decomposition therefore need checks on how a solver reaches its answer and feedback that locates the error. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/SIKAI-C/DecompGym.

items.title: Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation and a Large-Scale Multi-SKU Benchmark for Shampoo Bottle Surface Defect Detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industrial shampoo-bottle surface defect detection must operate across many stock keeping units (SKUs), where differences in bottle geometry, material, label layout, reflectance, and imaging conditions can substantially alter the appearance of the same defect. Existing industrial defect datasets rarely provide both instance-level defect annotations and product-variant identities, making it difficult to study SKU-aware detection under realistic manufacturing conditions. We introduce Bottle-SKU, a large-scale multi-SKU benchmark for shampoo bottle surface defect detection. Bottle-SKU contains 13,119 images, 20,419 instance-level bounding boxes, seven defect categories, and 48 bottle SKUs, enabling evaluation of both shared defect recognition and SKU-specific appearance variation. To address the challenge of SKU-specific appearance variation, we propose Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation (ProDMM). ProDMM constructs a visual prototype for each SKU from training images and predicts a soft SKU distribution for each input. The resulting prototype-conditioned representation dynamically generates low-rank Query/Value modulation for the visual backbone and residual conditioning for defect-text-to-visual attention, while preserving the pretrained Grounding DINO detection pathway. The model is trained jointly with detection, SKU-domain classification, and modulation-regularization objectives. Experiments on Bottle-SKU and the public GC10-DET-SKU metallic surface defect dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of prototype-guided domain conditioning for industrial surface defect detection.

items.title: From Natural Language to Real Schematics: An Automated Workflow for Power Electronics Schematic Synthesis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing power electronics converters traditionally requires intensive human expertise across topology sizing, commercial component selection, circuit simulation verification, and schematic drafting. While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in electronic design automation (EDA), applying standalone LLMs directly to board-level power electronics schematic synthesis suffers from severe engineering hallucinations, including inaccurate analytical sizing, fabricated or mismatched component part numbers, violated voltage derating margins, and broken topological connectivity. In this paper, we propose a Bounded Dual-Loop Automated Schematic Synthesis Framework that translates natural language specifications into verified, editable KiCad schematics and manufacturing deliverables. Our workflow integrates six stages across three functional columns: (1) requirement parsing and knowledge-driven power stage synthesis covering non-isolated (Buck, Boost) and isolated/resonant (Flyback, DAB, half-bridge LLC) topologies; (2) contract- and evidence-coordinated component selection grounded in distributor APIs and OEM datasheets, coupled with closed-loop ngspice transient verification and stress feedback; and (3) modular control hardware integration and multi-format deliverable generation featuring native KiCad netlist round-trip verification. End-to-end case studies on a 24-36V to 12V,2A Buck converter (29 positions, 83 verified terminals) and an isolated 48V to 24V, 0.5A, Dual-Active Bridge (DAB) converter (87 positions, 341 verified terminals), alongside comparative evaluations against a Vanilla LLM baseline, demonstrate that our framework improves component verification coverage from 22.2 to 98.6, nominal value consistency from 0 to 97.7, and SPICE simulation pass rates from 0 to 100.

items.title: GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.

items.title: Disparity Laundering: Consensus Without Fairness in Clinical Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical large language models are increasingly fielded as multi-agent teams, on the assumption that deliberation averages out individual error. It does not average out bias. Across a full factorial of five model families and four aggregation topologies on 120 real MIMIC-IV emergency cases under counterfactual demographic swaps, no configuration neutralizes the disparity: all 20 cells commit the direction of their agents' independent answers, giving Black patients more acute triage. Every model has a topology that amplifies its baseline gap, but which one varies by model, so no design is reliably safe or reliably amplifying: the disparity is relocated, never removed. Late-stage fixes fail: fairness instructions and demographic masking leave the gap untouched, and per-agent self-debiasing widens it, because the bias is already encoded in the agents' ordinary clinical numbers. We call this disparity laundering; the audits now applied to clinical AI, per model, per output, per version, can certify the parts but never the committed decision. Interventions close the gap exactly when they make counterfactual versions visible inside the system and pool them, through deliberation, into the committed decision. A diverse-perspective ensemble does both while keeping the team, with no retraining or architectural change: the disparity falls by 67 to 94% where all five perspectives pool at every round, and the one topology that never pools them is the one it cannot reliably repair. Medical multi-agent systems do not filter demographic bias; they launder it into plausible decisions no single-version audit can catch, and the only defense is to make the bias visible.

items.title: Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rubrics enable reward assignment on tasks without verifiable answers, but are expensive to manually produce from scratch. We present Rubricon, a pipeline that generates discriminative rubrics without requiring human preference labels, rubric annotation, or generator-model training. Using any LLM, Rubricon samples multiple rubrics, selects the most discriminative candidate, adds criteria to capture overlooked requirements or response flaws, and prunes criteria that are misaligned or shallow. Alongside LLM self-critique and test-time scaling, Rubricon uses observed criterion pass rates on example model responses to guide refinement. Across five professional, consumer, clinical, and general-use LLM benchmarks, Rubricon produces rubrics whose scores of frontier LLM responses exhibit 9% greater alignment with labor-intensive expert-authored rubrics, compared to the best alternative synthetic rubric generation method among RRD, QSRG, OpenRubrics, and agentic generation via harnesses like Codex. On HealthBench, post-training a Qwen3.5-9B model with Rubricon rubrics yields 4.5% better performance than training with rubrics from the strongest alternative synthetic rubric generator, RRD.

items.title: FACTS-MAS: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Adaptive Forecasting from Heterogeneous Evidence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world forecasting often requires integrating heterogeneous evidence whose predictive value varies across horizons, operating regimes, and domains. We introduce FACTS-MAS, a domain-agnostic multi-agent forecasting framework that decomposes evidence into specialized channels for temporal dynamics, exogenous context, seasonality, structural information, and discrete events. Each agent generates an independently testable forecast through a common interface, while leakage-safe historical validation measures its predictive skill relative to a naive reference. These skill estimates are used to weight and combine agent forecasts, so that uninformative evidence is either removed or downweighted rather than forced to participate. A calibration procedure selects domain-specific constant means based on historical validation folds. We evaluate FACTS-MAS on weekly for-sale housing inventory from Zillow and weekly unemployment insurance claims from FRED, for 15 U.S. metropolitan areas at 4-, 8-, and 13-week forecasting horizons. Our method outperforms both a naive last-value forecast method and the TimesFM foundation model. However, a factor-adjusted exponential smoothing model performs as well as the fused forecast. The evidence therefore supports FACTS-MAS as a systematic protocol for testing, calibrating, and recomposing evidence channels before assembling them into the strongest single model for a specific application domain. Code, data, and results are available at https://github.com/Madumita24/FACTS-MAS.

items.title: Verification-Guided Retrosynthesis: Reaction Feedback and Evidence Timing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrosynthesis planning seeks synthesis routes from purchasable starting materials to a target molecule. Search over predicted reactions can connect a target to available materials, yet an infeasible reaction can invalidate the resulting route. Evaluating route quality only after search has finished cannot correct errors made during search. We introduce Verification-Guided Reflow (VGR), incorporating reaction verification as a decision action in AND/OR search. Verification results are represented as binary verdicts; queries are scheduled from the search structure, and acquired verdicts exclude reactions or adjust search priorities. We define verified solvability as the fraction of targets for which a complete route accepted stepwise by the verifier is found. On Retro190, feeding verification results into search increases verified solvability from 51.1% to 62.6% relative to route evaluation without feedback. Further controlled experiments show that earlier verification and immediate prioritization of accepted reactions each improve route discovery, yet combining them performs worse than either change alone. We therefore propose early pruning and delayed guidance: rejected reactions are pruned immediately, while accepted reactions gain search priority when processed as part of a complete candidate route. In a separate comparison with the verification scheduling rule fixed, this strategy increases verified solvability from 61.1% with immediate guidance to 71.1%, using fewer proposal calls and unique verifier queries.

items.title: Inner-Learning: From Hand-Coded Beliefs to Declarative Knowledge in Trick-Taking Games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a declarative approach to belief-state modeling in trick-taking card games. Starting from a state-of-the-art Skat player, we automatically extract its hand-coded inference rules into a domain-specific language built on the primitive $\neg\mathsf{holds}(P,C)$, denoting that player $P$ cannot hold any card in set $C$. Round-trip code generation verifies that the extracted rules reproduce the original engine's intended behavior, up to three audited bugs in the original that the declarative engine corrects. We then grow the rule base through symmetric derivation and annotation of an expert strategy document---unifying code, symmetry, and expertise in one representation. We extend the knowledge representation with \emph{cardinality constraints}: at-most-$k$ and at-least-$k$ bounds on the cards a player holds from a named group, expressed in the same declarative language and enforced at world-generation time. Confidence parameters connect symbolic rules to probabilistic belief updates. Self-play evaluation shows the declarative engine measurably improving winning percentage and score over the original hand-coded engine, with the extracted rules, the human-annotated rules, and the cardinality constraints each contributing to the effect.

items.title: Game-Theoretic Foundations for Undiscounted Bisimulation Metrics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bisimulation metrics offer a principled notion of task-relevant state similarity in reinforcement learning, but existing constructions and methods are largely confined to discounted MDPs, where contraction arguments ensure well-defined fixed points and downstream guarantees. We develop a unified foundation for bisimulation metrics in undiscounted settings, that is total- and average-reward problems, by replacing the standard operator-centric view with a game-centric one: we interpret prior metric operators as Bellman-Shapley operators of zero-sum turn-based games and define metrics as the corresponding game value functions, yielding unique definitions even when $\gamma=1$. This game-theoretic foundation facilitates transfer of dynamic-programming theory and algorithms. We also use this game-centric perspective to characterize how metric finiteness depends on structural properties of the underlying MDP and motivate certain directed metrics that remain finite in weakly communicating MDPs. We further introduce an abstract framework for modifying the games' action spaces, allowing general transition coupling sets, that recovers many existing metrics and guides new constructions. Finally, we prove that these metrics bound total-reward and, when the optimal gain is state-independent, optimal relative value differences. We also provide error and suboptimality guarantees for aggregation-based planning in total- and average-reward settings.

items.title: CHORD: Cross-Model Hallucination Detection via Relational Graph Discrimination [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38314v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hallucination detection is critical for deploying large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications. Due to strong empirical performance, internal representation-based methods have emerged as the prevailing direction for detecting hallucinations, yet they remain largely model-specific and often fail to generalize to unseen LLMs. In this paper, we study an important yet underexplored problem, termed cross-model hallucination detection (CMHD), which aims to train hallucination detectors on source LLMs while ensuring performance on unseen target LLMs. The core challenge of CMHD lies in cross-model representation heterogeneity: hidden states from different LLMs exhibit severe semantic inconsistency, which limits the transferability of classical representation-based detectors. Through analysis and empirical validation, we show that relational structures over layers, tokens, and features capture transferable detection signals despite semantic inconsistency. Based on this observation, we propose cross-model hallucination detection via heterogeneity-oriented relational discrimination (CHORD), a relational graph discrimination framework that represents hidden states as joint relational graphs over layers, tokens, and features. It feeds these graphs into relation-aware attention to obtain structure-aware features, and uses meta-learning to shape these features toward transferable detection signals. Extensive experiments show that CHORD outperforms representative detection methods in cross-model generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/MiracleworkerD/CHORD.

items.title: Can LLMs Faithfully Solve Ontology Engineering Tasks? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ontological knowledge underpins large language model (LLM) performance on knowledge-intensive tasks. However, existing evaluations of LLMs' ontological understanding largely rely on behavioral correctness, leaving the underlying mechanisms unexplained. Existing mechanistic interpretability work has largely focused on instance-level factual knowledge, leaving ontological knowledge under-explored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MIOE, a causal-abstraction benchmark that evaluates interchange interventions for two ontology engineering tasks: entity typing and subsumption prediction. MIOE tests whether learned internal intervention targets can change an ontology-level target answer while preserving class-specific auxiliary information. Across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B, we evaluate SAE-, DBM-, and DAS-based methods, including multi-task and multi-layer variants. Distributed subspace methods give the strongest results and generalize across prompt settings, but the induced changes remain only partially separated from auxiliary class-specific information. Multi-task objectives and contiguous layer-window interventions improve this balance, while class-level analyses reveal substantial variation across ontology classes. These results suggest that ontological predictions are mechanistically accessible in LLMs, although current methods do not yet isolate a cleanly disentangled causal mechanism for ontological knowledge.

items.title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Financial agents must form forecasts and investment judgments from decision-time evidence, with predictions evaluated against subsequent outcomes. Existing benchmarks assess financial knowledge, research workflows, or forecasting, but evaluating the full research process requires a strictly frozen information set and professional evaluation criteria. We introduce Investor's Last Exam (ILE), an equity-research benchmark led by experienced buy-side investors and fund managers. Its three components are a versioned financial database spanning 3.43 million document versions and nine source categories, supplemented by structured market data, with validated timestamps governing retrieval and computation; a task taxonomy organized around professional analyst deliverables; and an expert-led framework linking scoring criteria to sources, calculations, and assumptions through financial dependency graphs. Evaluation spans 86 assignments and jointly assesses research quality, forecast accuracy, and simulated investment performance. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead overall at 68.1 and 66.9 out of 100, yet even Astra scores only 52.5 on Forecast & Model. Our results show that even state-of-the-art models fail to translate overall research capability into predictive performance. ILE shifts the evaluation unit from isolated capabilities to the evidence--assumption--judgment chain, allowing researchers to locate where analytical advantages fail to translate into forecasts and investment judgments, and providing a traceable, diagnostic foundation for training and evaluating financial agents.

items.title: Encode Once, Answer Many: Internalizing Context via Parametric Flow [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are typically adapted to a task either by placing knowledge in the input context, which keeps it external and re-encodes it on every call, or by fine-tuning, which internalizes it but demands a costly round of optimization per task. We aim to internalize the knowledge carried by a context directly into model parameters, without per-task optimization and without keeping the context in the input at inference time. To this end, we propose CLIK, a context-conditioned parameter generator that maps a given context to LoRA parameters for internalizing knowledge in a single forward pass through a Transformer encoder with cross-attention, requiring no test-time gradient updates. Once the generated LoRA is inserted into a frozen base model, the model answers downstream queries from the query alone, having internalized the context into its weights rather than re-reading it. Because the adapter depends only on the context, it is generated once and reused for every query on the same document, so the cost of reading that document is amortized across queries. On document question answering, CLIK substantially improves over the no-context base model and outperforms existing hypernetwork-based generators, while remaining behind a base model that reads the context directly, and it carries over to multi-turn dialogue without any multi-turn-specific training. Analysis further shows that the context-dependent part of the generated adapter concentrates in a compact and specific substructure.

items.title: Compute Has Shape: Self-Morphing the Internal Computation of Frozen LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time scaling improves large language models through additional computation, but how to adapt the topology of internal computation to individual inputs remains underexplored. Existing approaches largely fix recurrent or parallel architectures during training, or reconfigure frozen models along a single structural axis. We introduce SelfMorph, which makes computational shape an input-dependent inference-time decision. It unifies the original forward path (BASE), serial reuse of a layer span (REPEAT), and local branching and merging of perturbed hidden states (BRANCH) in a unified space parameterized by type, location, and intensity. Since they offer complementary benefits rather than uniform dominance, we use a lightweight selector that reads the backbone's depth-wise hidden state trajectory on the prompt to choose a morphology before response generation. We train the selector by distilling utility-based distribution from offline morphing that jointly account for task performance and computational cost. Evaluated on three LLMs spanning 4B-27B, SelfMorph achieves a 8.06% mean relative improvement on five in-distribution benchmarks and 4.45% on four unseen benchmarks. It achieves the strongest performance in 24 of 27 settings. These findings identify input-adaptive computational topology as a complementary axis of test-time scaling beyond generating more tokens. Our code is available at https://github.com/creator-xi/SelfMorph.

items.title: SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides coarse supervision for long-horizon LLM agents: failed trajectories may contain correct steps, while successful trajectories can contain errors. Trajectory-level skills can also shift teacher preferences at unrelated steps, introducing off-target distillation signals. We introduce SCOPE, a framework for Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation. After a supervised warm-up, the policy analyzes its own trajectories, generates step-specific hindsight skills, and distills their guidance only at selected error steps. A bounded signed teacher-student coefficient stabilizes auxiliary updates while preserving positive reinforcement and negative correction. A success-relative pairwise length reward further encourages efficient task completion. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple model backbones. With Qwen2.5-3B, SCOPE achieves 97.7% success on ALFWorld and 85.2% on WebShop, outperforming SEED by 5.9 and 6.3 percentage points, respectively. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, SCOPE reaches 89.6% success, improving over GRPO by 23.2 percentage points with 46.7% fewer interactions. Scaling to Qwen3-32B, SCOPE achieves 99.2% success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 94.0% on unseen tasks.

items.title: Masked Erosion: How Acceptance Gates Lose Redundant Safeguards in Self-Improving Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-improving LLM agents edit their own harness, the prompts and rules around a fixed model, and keep an edit only if an acceptance gate scores it higher on a batch of tasks. Such a gate sees what the harness does under the current model, not what it would still prevent if one safeguard failed. When safeguards overlap, deleting one is masked: the others still block the harm, so the gate decides on task success alone and redundancy erodes unseen. We measure harm for every subset of four written safeguards in two agent environments and run 411 improvement loops under ten gate rules, mostly as controlled deletion experiments, plus three runs of the GEPA optimizer. A deletion behind another working safeguard adds almost no observable harm. A paired significance test blocks deletions that pass by chance but not deletions that genuinely raise task success, and a larger evaluation batch lets it delete cheaper safeguards: at the same cost, 20-task batches kept every harness protected while 40-task batches lost all six. Large harm audits prevent exposure but not the loss of depth, which turns into harm when the harness is reused with a weaker model. GEPA kept every safety rule verbatim, yet two of its three final harnesses misused credentials under a weaker model. A statistical model frozen before the runs predicts where each gate's protection breaks as safeguard cost and batch size change, and freezing safety text or auditing one-layer ablations preserves depth.

items.title: Agent Transfer Protocol: Server-Mediated Agent-to-Agent Communication Architecture for the Agentic Web [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Agentic Web needs to support continuous collaboration among agents from different organizations. These collaborative relationships may span multiple tasks, network connections and execution instances. Such interactions require stable communication entries, message reception when instances are offline, and source verification after delayed reading. How to organize these responsibilities so that cross domain communication does not depend on specific execution instances being continuously online is a key issue for building long term agent interaction infrastructure. We propose ATP (Agent Transfer Protocol), a cross organization agent communication protocol adopting a domain mediated architecture. In this architecture, administrative domains maintain stable addresses and receiving entries for logical agents. The domain servers of both parties continuously undertake cross domain transmission. The receiving domain verifies and saves messages for execution instances to read later. The sending domain signs the complete message envelope. This allows the receiving instance to independently reverify the domain source and content integrity after the original connection ends, provided the original verification public key is still trusted and obtainable. We implemented an ATP prototype and evaluated it through a controlled cross organization LLM agent workflow, mechanism checks and latency measurements. The workflow completed subsequent business processing after instances went offline or were replaced. The independent verifier successfully verified the domain source and content integrity of saved messages. Latency measurements further quantified the communication and processing overhead introduced by the continuous mediation of domain servers.

items.title: Governance-Aware Federated Learning for Multi-Agent AI Systems: A Policy-Driven Framework for Trustworthy Collaborative AI [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without exchanging raw data, but conventional FL provides limited runtime governance, evidence verification, fairness assessment, explainability monitoring, and auditability. This paper proposes Governance-Aware Federated Learning (GAFL), which combines independent governance-evidence verification, temporal trust, fairness and explanation assessment, anomaly detection, policy enforcement, normalized aggregation, and tamper-evident audit logging. Client-reported governance values are authenticated, bound to their submitted model updates, and independently recomputed before aggregation. A cross-silo prototype with 10 participants was evaluated on the Adult Income dataset under honest, benign non-IID, biased-data, malicious-update, non-compliant, falsified-evidence, and mixed-threat scenarios. Four methods were compared across five random seeds: FedAvg, FedAvg with anomaly filtering, GAFL without independent verification, and complete GAFL. Complete GAFL intervened on all affected participants at the final round across the evaluated risk scenarios, including identifying 100% of falsified-evidence participants, whereas GAFL without verification identified none of the falsified-evidence participants. Final macro-F1 ranged from 0.7520 to 0.7733 across GAFL scenarios. Complete GAFL required 173.67 plus or minus 26.94 ms of governance processing per round, compared with 3.82 plus or minus 0.79 ms for FedAvg. A strict demographic-parity threshold also caused frequent interventions for honest participants, demonstrating a significant fairness-policy and utility trade-off.

items.title: Predict the Reward, Not the World: World Reward Models for ML Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.38439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Search-based machine-learning (ML) agents improve a solution by writing candidate programs, executing them, and keeping the best. Execution gives the search reliable feedback, but a single run can take hours, and most runs end in programs the agent discards.
